title: Cover 2 vs Cover 3: How Quarterbacks Tell the Difference
description: The fastest pre-snap read a quarterback can make: count the deep safeties. How to tell Cover 2 from Cover 3, where each one is weak, and how to confirm it after the snap.
intro: Every pass play starts with one question: how many safeties are deep? Answer it before the snap and you already know where the open grass is likely to be. Cover 2 and Cover 3 are two of the most common coverages you will see, and telling them apart is one of the first reads every quarterback should master.

sections.h: Step one: count the deep safeties
p: Before you look at anything else, find the safeties. Are there two of them sitting deep, roughly over the hash marks and usually about 12 to 15 yards off the ball? Or is there one safety in the middle of the field?

Two high safeties usually means a two-deep coverage like Cover 2. One high safety usually means a one-deep coverage like Cover 3. Coaches call this "two-high" and "one-high," and it is the single most useful thing you can see before the snap. One note: two-high can also be Cover 4 (quarters). In Cover 4 the safeties usually sit a little shallower, around 10 to 12 yards, and the corners play off the ball instead of squatting.

In Cover 2, the two safeties each take a deep half of the field. Underneath them, five defenders play zones: the two corners, usually squatting in the flats, and three defenders (usually linebackers) across the middle.
Pre-snap clues for Cover 2: two safeties deep and wide, and corners often lined up closer to the line, sometimes with outside leverage, ready to jam the receiver and sink to the flat.
list: Two safeties deep, each over a hash
Corners shallow, often outside the receiver

p: Two defenders cannot cover the whole deep field, so Cover 2 has two soft spots. The first is the area along the sideline, deeper than the squatting corner and in front of the deep safety. Coaches call it "the hole." Corner routes and fade-stop routes attack it.
The second is the deep middle, between the two safeties. A receiver who splits them on a seam or post can get behind the linebackers and in front of the safeties.
In Cover 3, one safety plays the deep middle and the two corners each take a deep outside third. That leaves four defenders underneath, usually a mix of linebackers and the other safety or nickel.
Pre-snap clues for Cover 3: one safety in the middle of the field, corners playing off the receiver with depth, and an extra defender walked down near the box.
list: One safety deep in the middle
Corners off the ball, ready to bail deep

p: With three defenders deep, Cover 3 is harder to beat over the top, but the underneath zones are stretched. Quick throws to the flat, curl routes in front of the bailing corner, and seam routes that split the deep thirds all put stress on it.
Four vertical routes are a classic Cover 3 beater: four receivers going deep against three deep defenders forces the middle safety to pick one of the two seams, which leaves the other one open.
Defenses disguise. A two-high look can rotate into one-high at the snap, and the reverse. So treat your pre-snap read as a guess, then confirm it with your first look after the snap.

Watch the corners. If they sink and squat in the flat, think Cover 2. If they turn and run deep, think Cover 3 (or man coverage, if they stay glued to one receiver). Watch the safeties too: if one drives down toward the line late, the defense may have rotated into a one-high look.

Watch film with the sound off and pause every play right before the snap. Say out loud "one-high" or "two-high," then play the clip and check yourself. A few minutes a day builds the habit faster than you think.
You can also practice the read in the free QB Lab on this site, which shows you a defense and asks where the ball should go.

title: How to Read a Blitz Before the Snap
description: The pre-snap signs that a blitz is coming, and what a quarterback should do about it: hot reads, protection calls, and throwing to where the blitzer left.
intro: A blitz is the defense betting that it can get to you before you get the ball out. If you see it coming, that bet usually loses. Here are the signs to look for before the snap, and what to do once you see them.

sections.h: Sign 1: linebackers creeping toward the line
p: Linebackers usually line up a few yards off the ball, often around four to five. When one walks up into a gap, or inches forward as the play clock runs down, he may be coming. Linebackers standing right on the line over the center, in the A-gaps, are a strong warning sign.

sections.h: Sign 2: a safety rotating down late
p: A safety who drifts toward the line of scrimmage just before the snap is often either blitzing or replacing a linebacker who is. Watch for a safety cheating down from a two-high look into the box.

sections.h: Sign 3: tight coverage with no help
p: When defensive backs press your receivers and there is no safety deep, the defense is often playing man coverage behind a blitz. They are sending extra rushers and trusting their corners to hold up for a short time.

Rushers often give themselves away. A linebacker leaning forward with weight on his toes, eyes on the ball instead of the backfield, or a defensive back staring at the quarterback can all signal pressure.

sections.h: What to do when you see it
list: Count the rushers against your blockers. If they can bring more than you can block, someone has to throw quickly.
Know your hot read. Before every play, know which receiver you go to if a free rusher comes. Usually the ball goes to the area the blitzer just left.
Set the protection. Point out the Mike linebacker so your line knows who they are responsible for, and adjust the protection if your offense lets you.
Use your cadence. A hard count can make a creeping defender jump early or show his hand.
Get the ball out. Against a blitz, a quick completion beats holding the ball for the perfect throw.

p: Not every creeping linebacker blitzes. Good defenses show pressure and then back out. Use the signs to prepare, not to decide. Know your answer before the snap, then confirm what is actually coming after it.

title: 6 Quarterback Footwork Drills You Can Do on Your Own
description: Six quarterback footwork drills you can do alone with a ball and a few cones: drops, climbing the pocket, resetting your feet, and throwing on the move.
intro: Accuracy starts with your feet. A good throw needs a balanced base, and a balanced base comes from footwork you have repeated so often that you do not think about it. These six drills need only a football, a few cones or markers, and some open space.

p: Stand on a yard line as if it were the line of scrimmage. Take your three-step and five-step drops (or one-step and three-step from the shotgun), and finish each one balanced with your feet about shoulder-width apart.

Check yourself: are you landing on the balls of your feet, not your heels? Is your front shoulder pointing downfield, with your feet roughly perpendicular to the target? Do ten of each, slowly at first, then at game speed.

After your drop, take one or two short hitch steps forward, as if you are moving up into the pocket, then set your feet and throw. Many throws in a game come after a hitch, not straight off the drop, so practice the rhythm.

Set up two cones about three yards behind the line, a few yards apart, to act as edge rushers. Drop back, then step up between them, keeping your eyes downfield the whole time. Finish with a throw. This teaches you to escape edge pressure by moving forward, not by drifting backward, because the rushers' momentum carries them past you. If pressure comes up the middle instead, slide sideways rather than stepping into it.

Set up three targets: left, middle and right. Drop back, then have a partner call out a target, or pick one at random. Reset your feet so your front shoulder points at the new target, then step toward it as you throw. Throwing off a reset base is one of the biggest keys to accuracy across the field.

Roll out to your right, square your shoulders toward the target as you run, and throw on the move. Then do the same to your left, which is harder for right-handed quarterbacks and needs more practice. Keep the ball high and close to your chest while you run.

Quick feet help in a crowded pocket. Use an agility ladder, or just hop side to side and forward and back over a yard line, for 20 to 30 seconds at a time. Keep your knees bent and stay on the balls of your feet.

sections.h: How to fit it into your week
p: Ten to fifteen minutes of footwork, three or four times a week, adds up quickly. Film yourself with your phone once a week so you can compare your drops over time. Small fixes to your base show up as big improvements in accuracy.

title: The Quarterback Pre-Snap Checklist: 5 Things to See Before Every Snap
description: A simple five-step pre-snap routine for quarterbacks: count the safeties, check the corners, find the Mike, look for blitz tells, and know your hot read.
intro: The best quarterbacks make the game slower by doing the same thing before every snap. They look at the defense in the same order, every time, so nothing surprises them. Here is a simple five-step checklist you can start using at your next practice.

p: One high or two high? This tells you the coverage family before anything else. One deep safety usually means Cover 1 or Cover 3. Two deep safeties usually means Cover 2, Cover 4 or a two-high variation.

Are the corners pressed up on your receivers or playing off, and where are their eyes? Corners pressed tight and staring at the receiver often mean man coverage. Corners playing off and looking in at you often mean zone. This changes which routes are your best options.
Identify the middle linebacker and point him out so your offensive line knows how to set the protection. It also forces you to look at the second level of the defense, where blitzes often come from.
Linebackers creeping toward the line, a safety rotating down late, or defensive backs in tight coverage with no deep help can all signal pressure.
If the defense brings more rushers than you can block, where does the ball go? Decide this before the snap, not after. The answer is usually the area the extra rusher came from.

At first, this will feel slow. That is normal. Run through the checklist on every rep at practice, and while watching film, until you do it without thinking. Once it is a habit, you will see the defense in a second or two, and the game will feel slower.

title: How Quarterbacks Bounce Back After a Bad Play
description: Interceptions and bad throws happen to every quarterback. A simple next-play routine to reset your mind, stay confident, and lead your team after a mistake.
intro: Every quarterback throws interceptions. Every quarterback misses open receivers. What separates good quarterbacks is not avoiding mistakes, but how fast they recover from them. Your teammates are watching how you react, so the next play starts the second the last one ends.

p: A reset routine is a short, physical habit that tells your brain the last play is over. It might be wiping your hands on your towel, tapping your helmet, or clapping once. Do the same thing every time so it becomes automatic.
Pair it with one slow breath: in through your nose, out through your mouth, a little longer on the way out. A slow exhale helps calm your body when your heart rate is up.

Pick one or two words that point you forward, like "next one," "reset" or "see it, throw it." Say it to yourself after the routine. It replaces the replay running in your head with an instruction for what comes next.

sections.h: Learn from it later, not now
p: During the game, you only need the quick lesson: "the safety rotated down" or "I stared down my receiver." Save the full analysis for film. Trying to fix everything in the middle of a drive pulls your focus away from the next play.

Your teammates take their cue from you. Walk back to the huddle with your head up. Take responsibility if it was your fault, briefly, and then call the next play with confidence. Teammates trust a quarterback who stays steady after a mistake.

sections.h: Practice it before you need it
p: Use your routine at practice after every bad rep, not just in games. The more often you practice resetting, the faster it works when it matters.
If stress or anxiety about football starts to affect your sleep, your mood or your life outside the game, talk to a parent, a coach or a counselor. That is a strength, not a weakness.
